Understanding Alzheimer's Disease
Understanding

Alzheimer'sDisease

What it is, how it progresses, and how we can help.

Presented by Ayse ChumberFall 2026
Welcome everyone. Today I will talk about Alzheimer's disease: what it is, how it progresses, how it is diagnosed and treated, and how families can support people who live with it.
What is Alzheimer's disease?

A progressive brain disease that slowly damages memory, thinking and behavior.

Over time, everyday tasks become harder
Cooking Driving Managing money
!

It is not a normal part of aging.Forgetting a name now and then is normal. Alzheimer's is a disease.

Alzheimer's is a progressive disease, which means it gets worse over time. It damages memory, thinking and behavior, and slowly makes everyday tasks like cooking, driving or managing money harder. The key message: it is not a normal part of getting older.
Important facts

Three facts to remember

#1

most common cause of dementia

Dementia is the general term for losing memory and thinking skills. Alzheimer's causes most cases.

65+

age when symptoms usually begin

Most people develop symptoms after age 65, but aging alone does not cause it.

0

cures available today

Treatment can still help manage symptoms, and some new medicines can slow the disease.

Three facts to remember. One: Alzheimer's is the most common cause of dementia. Two: symptoms usually begin after age 65. Three: there is no cure yet, but treatments can help manage symptoms and, for some people, slow the disease.
Signs and symptoms

The early signs are easy to miss

These are the most common signs. Early on they are easy to mistake for normal forgetfulness. The difference is that they keep happening and get in the way of daily life. (Tip: click a card to highlight it while you talk about it.)
Stages

Alzheimer's progresses in three stages

Violet = affected areas
Early stage

Mild memory loss. The person can still live mostly independently.

In the brain

Changes begin in the hippocampus, the brain's memory center.

IndependenceMostly independent
Alzheimer's moves through three stages. Early: mild memory loss, but the person is mostly independent. Middle: memory loss and confusion get worse and they need help with daily activities. Late: they may lose the ability to communicate, recognize others, walk, eat or care for themselves. (Click Early, Middle, Late to show how damage spreads through the brain.)
Causes and risk factors

The exact cause is unknown. Some factors raise the risk.

Can't be changed

Age

The strongest risk factor, especially after 65.

Genetics

Family history and the APOE-ε4 gene variant can increase risk.

Can be influenced

Healthy habits help

Heart & metabolic health

High blood pressure, diabetes, heart disease

Physical inactivity

Too little regular movement

Smoking

Damages blood vessels, including the brain's

Poor sleep

Long-term poor sleep quality

Head injuries

Serious or repeated injuries

Source: Nystuen et al., 2024
Scientists don't know the exact cause, but several factors raise the risk. Age is the strongest, and genes like APOE-ε4 play a role. These can't be changed. Others can be influenced: heart and metabolic health, physical activity, smoking, sleep and head injuries. What is good for the heart is also good for the brain.
What happens inside the brain?

Two proteins go wrong, and neurons stop talking

Healthy neurons · signals flowing
Sources: Liu et al., 2024; Nystuen et al., 2024
This is what happens at the level of brain cells. Press Play, or click each step. 1: amyloid-beta protein forms plaques between neurons. 2: tau protein forms tangles inside neurons. 3: the connections between neurons are damaged, so signals stop. 4: brain cells die and parts of the brain shrink, which causes the memory problems we see.
How Alzheimer's is diagnosed

No single test. Doctors put the pieces together.

Why early?

An early diagnosis gives the person and family time to plan, and the newest medicines only work in the early stage.

Source: Liu et al., 2024
There is no single test for Alzheimer's. Doctors combine several: medical and family history, memory and thinking tests, physical and neurological exams with blood tests to rule out other causes, brain scans like MRI, CT or PET, and when needed, biomarker tests that detect amyloid-beta and tau. Diagnosing early matters because the newest medicines only work in the early stage.
Treatment

There is no cure yet, but treatment helps

Medicine

Symptom medicines may temporarily improve memory and thinking.

New medicines may slow the disease in some people in the early stage.

Daily life

Daily routines reduce confusion and stress.

Exercise and social activity support overall health.

Family and caregivers provide essential support.

There is no cure yet, but treatment helps in two ways. Medicines can ease symptoms, and newer ones may slow the disease early on. Daily life matters just as much: routines reduce confusion, exercise and social activity support health, and family support is essential.
Medications

How the medicines work

DonepezilBrand name: Aricept

Stops an enzyme from breaking down acetylcholine, a chemical messenger for memory. More messages get through.

May temporarily help memory and thinking

Important: none of these medicines cure Alzheimer's, they are not right for everyone, and all can have side effects. Lecanemab and donanemab need regular MRI scans to check for brain swelling or small bleeds.

Sources: van Dyck et al., 2023; Sims et al., 2023
Donepezil, brand name Aricept, stops an enzyme from breaking down acetylcholine, a messenger the brain uses for memory, so more signals get through. It may help memory and thinking for a while. Lecanemab (Leqembi) and donanemab (Kisunla) are antibodies that help the body clear amyloid plaques. In clinical trials they slowed decline in early Alzheimer's by about 27% for lecanemab, and up to 35% for donanemab in people with lower tau levels, over about 18 months. None of them cure the disease, they are not suitable for everyone, and they can cause side effects. (Press "Give medicine" to show the effect.)
Supporting patients

Small habits that make a big difference

Speak calmly and simply

Short sentences, one idea at a time. Give them enough time to answer.

Keep a familiar routine

Same daily rhythm. Use calendars, reminders and labels.

Make the home safe

Prevent falls and wandering.

Always with patience, kindness and respect.

Supporting someone with Alzheimer's is about small, daily habits. Speak calmly in short sentences and give them time to respond. Keep a familiar routine and use calendars, reminders and labels. Make the home safe to prevent falls and wandering. And above all: patience, kindness and respect.
Caregivers

Caregivers need care too

Rest

Take regular breaks to avoid burnout.

Share

Divide responsibilities among family members.

Ask for help

Doctors, support groups and local services can help.

Be patient

With the person you care for, and with yourself.

A rested caregiver gives better care.

Caring for someone with Alzheimer's is demanding, so caregivers need care too. They should rest, share responsibilities with family, ask for help from doctors, support groups and services, and be patient with the person and with themselves.
Conclusion

Alzheimer's changes the brain and everyday life, but we can make a difference.

Early diagnosis→The right treatment→Ongoing support=Quality of life & dignity
Thank you.Questions?
To conclude: Alzheimer's is a progressive brain disorder that affects memory, thinking and daily life. There is no cure yet, but early diagnosis, the right treatment and ongoing support from family, caregivers and healthcare professionals can improve quality of life and protect the person's dignity. Thank you. I'm happy to take questions.
